meta.title: Who really said "In a democracy, the people get the government they deserve"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Tocqueville. Joseph de Maistre wrote it in an 1811 letter from Saint Petersburg — and his maxim was about every nation, not about democracies.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In a democracy, the people get the government they deserve'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote files it under Misattributed. The maxim is Joseph de Maistre's, from letter 76, Saint Petersburg, 15/27 August 1811.

answer.label: Not Tocqueville — actually Joseph de Maistre
answer.authorDates: 1753–1821 · Savoyard diplomat, envoy at Saint Petersburg 1803–1817
answer.sourceLine: Tocqueville never wrote this. The maxim belongs to Joseph de Maistre — Toute nation a le gouvernement qu’elle mérite — set down as numbered point 2° of letter 76, written at Saint Petersburg on 15/27 August 1811 about Alexander I’s new constitutional laws. Even de Maistre’s sentence says every nation, not in a democracy; the familiar English wording is a later reshaping with no identified source in either writer.

source.excerpt: 2° Toute nation a le gouvernement qu’elle mérite. De longues réflexions, et une longue expérience payée bien cher, m’ont convaincu de cette vérité comme d’une proposition de mathématiques. Toute loi est donc inutile, et même funeste (quelque excellente qu’elle puisse être en elle-même), si la nation n’est pas digne de la loi et faite pour la loi.
trail: Wikiquote files “In a democracy, the people get the government they deserve” in the Misattributed section of its Tocqueville page ↗, with the note that it was Joseph de Maistre who wrote in 1811 “Every nation gets the government it deserves.”

Wikiquote’s de Maistre page ↗ gives the French — Toute nation a le gouvernement qu’elle mérite — as letter 76 on Russia’s new constitutional laws, dated 27 August 1811, notes English variants including “In a democracy people get the leaders they deserve,” and records the misattributions to Tocqueville and Lincoln.

The sentence is legible in the scan: Lettres et opuscules inédits, tome premier (Paris: A. Vaton, 1861) ↗ prints letter 76 headed “Saint-Pétersbourg, 15 (27) août 1811,” with the maxim as numbered point 2° on page 264 and repeated later in the same letter as ma maxime.
Searching the Henry Reeve translation of Tocqueville’s Democracy in America — volume 1 ↗ and volume 2 ↗ — turns up no sentence about a people or nation getting the government it deserves.
source.excerptNote: A plain working rendering: “Every nation has the government it deserves. Long reflection, and long experience paid for dearly, have convinced me of this truth as of a proposition in mathematics. Every law is therefore useless, and even disastrous — however excellent in itself — if the nation is not worthy of the law and made for the law.” De Maistre returns to the same sentence later in the letter, calling it ma maxime.

author.name: Joseph de Maistre
author.heading: Who was Joseph de Maistre?
author.bio: Joseph de Maistre was a Savoyard lawyer and diplomat who represented the King of Piedmont–Sardinia at the court of Alexander I in Saint Petersburg from 1803 to 1817. A leading counter-Enlightenment voice, he held monarchy to be the only durable form of government and blamed the Terror on rationalism’s rejection of Christianity. The maxim now quoted at democratic electorates was written by a man who doubted that a written constitution could improve a nation not already fit for one — “every law is therefore useless, and even disastrous … if the nation is not worthy of the law.”

misattribution.heading: How it ended up with Tocqueville
misattribution.intro: Tocqueville is the default signature for any tidy-sounding aphorism about democracy, so this one drifted to him. It is not his — and the man who did write it would have been startled to see it used as a lesson for voters.

items.why: Wikiquote’s Tocqueville page ↗ carries “In a democracy, the people get the government they deserve” in its Misattributed section, with the note that Joseph de Maistre wrote in 1811 “Every nation gets the government it deserves.” Searching the Henry Reeve translation of Democracy in America, volume 1 ↗ and volume 2 ↗, turns up no sentence of this kind.

Wikiquote ↗ records that the maxim is popularly misattributed to better-known commentators “such as Alexis de Tocqueville and Abraham Lincoln.” Lincoln is the standard second home for any democratic-sounding line in English.

De Maistre wrote toute nation — every nation — in a letter about autocratic Russia, not about democracies, and not about “the people” as an electorate. You can read the sentence in its place in the 1861 scan of the letters ↗. Wikiquote lists the “democracy” form only as one of several loose English renderings, with no translator named.

misattribution.truthLine: The maxim is Joseph de Maistre’s, written from Saint Petersburg on 15/27 August 1811 and printed as letter 76 in Lettres et opuscules inédits (1861), page 264 ↗ — and it was aimed at Russia under Alexander I, not at any democracy.

context.heading: What the letter was actually about
lead: Writing from Saint Petersburg in the summer of 1811, de Maistre was reacting to Alexander I’s new constitutional laws and the reorganisation of the Russian Senate. His argument runs in numbered points: first, that some true things should never be written into law at all (expressa nocent, non expressa non nocent), and then, as point two, the sentence that outlived everything else he wrote that day — every nation has the government it deserves, a truth of which long experience “paid for dearly” had convinced him as firmly as a proposition in mathematics.

The point was not a rebuke to voters. There were no voters. De Maistre was a monarchist telling a correspondent that Russia could not be improved by importing a European-style constitution, because a law is useless — even disastrous — if the nation is not made for it. He liked the line enough to come back to it later in the same letter, calling it ma maxime, my maxim.
context.detailsSummary: Why the “in a democracy” version is the giveaway
detailsBody: De Maistre’s subject is toute nation — every nation, of any kind, under any regime. The popular English form narrows it to democracies and swaps “nation” for “the people,” which turns a claim about national character under autocracy into a scolding of electorates. That is roughly the opposite of what the letter argues, and it is also why the line sounds like Tocqueville: the democracy framing was grafted on later.

Wikiquote records several competing English renderings of the same French sentence, including “Every country has the government it deserves” and “In a democracy people get the leaders they deserve.” No translator is named for any of them, which is the usual signature of a saying that travelled by repetition rather than through a book.
